headings.title: Introduction and Principles of the Oral Route
headings.content: The oral route of drug administration is the most common, convenient, and cost-effective method of delivering medications to patients. In clinical nursing practice across Nigeria and globally, administering medications by mouth involves swallowing drugs so they can enter the gastrointestinal (GI) tract and subsequently systemic circulation. The fundamental principle governing oral administration is relying on the patient's intact swallowing reflex and functioning GI system. Once ingested, most oral drugs dissolve in the stomach or intestines and are absorbed through the mucosal lining into the portal circulation, where they pass through the liver before reaching the rest of the body. Nurses must understand that this process subjects drugs to the 'first-pass metabolism,' a phenomenon where the concentration of a drug is significantly reduced before it reaches systemic circulation. Factors such as gastric pH, presence of food, intestinal motility, and liver enzyme function can greatly influence drug bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy. As nursing students, grasping these physiological principles is crucial for predicting how a patient will respond to oral pharmacotherapy, ensuring that medications are given under conditions that optimize absorption while minimizing adverse gastrointestinal effects. Proper assessment of the patient's readiness and ability to take medications orally is the foundational step in preventing complications like aspiration and therapeutic failure.

headings.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Oral Medication
headings.content: Administering medications via the oral route presents a distinct set of clinical advantages and disadvantages that every nursing student must master for safe practice. Among the primary advantages are convenience, economic production, and ease of self-administration, which promotes high patient compliance. Unlike parenteral routes, oral medications are non-invasive, reducing patient anxiety and eliminating the risk of localized tissue injury or blood-borne pathogen transmission associated with needles. Furthermore, oral administration is generally safer because, in the event of an accidental overdose or acute toxicity, interventions such as activated charcoal administration, gastric lavage, or emesis can often be performed to retrieve unabsorbed medication. However, the oral route also has notable disadvantages. The onset of drug action is typically much slower compared to intravenous or intramuscular injections, making oral drugs unsuitable for acute medical emergencies. Absorption rates can be unpredictable due to variables like stomach contents, pH, and motility. Additionally, the aforementioned first-pass effect can deactivate a large portion of an active drug ingredient. Oral medications can also irritate the gastric mucosa, cause unpleasant tastes, or stain teeth. Crucially, the oral route is completely contraindicated in patients who are unconscious, experiencing severe nausea and vomiting, have impaired swallowing reflexes, or have gastrointestinal obstructions.

headings.title: Common Forms of Oral Medications
headings.content: Oral medications are manufactured in a wide variety of solid, liquid, and semi-solid dosage forms to accommodate different pharmacological needs and patient populations. Solid forms include tablets, which are compressed powders; caplets, which are shaped like capsules for easier swallowing; and capsules, which enclose medication in a gelatin shell. Some solid forms are specially formulated, such as enteric-coated tablets designed to resist stomach acid and dissolve in the alkaline environment of the small intestine to protect the gastric lining, and sustained-release (SR) or extended-release (ER) capsules that release the active drug slowly over an extended period. It is vital that nurses never crush enteric-coated or sustained-release medications, as doing so destroys their special delivery mechanisms, leading to potential toxicity or drug inactivation. Liquid oral preparations include syrups (concentrated sugar solutions), elixirs (sweetened hydroalcoholic liquids), suspensions (mixtures containing undissolved drug particles that must be shaken thoroughly before use), and emulsions. Liquids are particularly useful for pediatric and geriatric patients who struggle to swallow pills. Nurses must use accurate measuring devices, such as calibrated oral syringes or medicine cups, rather than household kitchen spoons, to ensure precise dosage delivery.

headings.title: Pre-Administration Assessment and Preparation
headings.content: Before administering any oral medication, comprehensive pre-administration assessment and preparation are critical nursing responsibilities. The nurse must first review the medical record and the prescriber's order, verifying the patient's name, drug name, dosage, route, and timing against the medication administration record (MAR). Assessment includes checking the patient's allergy history, current vital signs, laboratory results (such as renal or hepatic function markers that affect drug metabolism), and any specific contraindications. The nurse must physically assess the patient's ability to swallow, level of consciousness, and presence of conditions like nausea, vomiting, or recent gastrointestinal surgery. When preparing the medication, the nurse should practice aseptic technique and work in a well-lit medication room to prevent medication errors. Solid medications should be dispensed from the stock container directly into a medication cup without touching them with bare hands. For liquid medications, the medicine cup must be placed on a flat, eye-level surface, and the liquid poured to the base of the meniscus. If calculations are required, such as converting milligrams to milliliters, the nurse must double-check the math and, when in doubt, consult a senior colleague or pharmacist. Thorough preparation ensures that potential errors are caught before the drug ever reaches the patient's bedside.

headings.title: The Rights of Medication Administration
headings.content: Safe medication administration hinges on strict adherence to the established 'Rights' of medication administration. While traditionally known as the 'Five Rights' (right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, and right time), modern nursing practice often expands this framework to include the right documentation, right reason, right response, right education, and the patient's right to refuse. The right patient must be verified using at least two unique identifiers, such as checking the patient's hospital identification band and asking them to state their full name and date of birth, rather than relying solely on room numbers. The right drug and right dose involve comparing the medication label against the MAR three times: when retrieving the medication, when preparing it, and just before administering it at the bedside. The right route ensures the drug is given orally as prescribed, rather than accidentally via another route. The right time ensures therapeutic blood levels are maintained consistently. The right reason requires the nurse to understand why the patient is receiving the medication, while the right response involves monitoring the patient afterward to see if the drug achieved its desired effect. Finally, patient education empowers the individual to understand what they are taking, and respecting the right to refuse underscores ethical nursing care.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Procedure for Administering Oral Medications
headings.content: Executing the step-by-step procedure for administering oral medications requires meticulous clinical technique and patient interaction. The nurse begins by gathering all necessary supplies, performing hand hygiene, and preparing the medications in accordance with safety standards. Upon entering the patient's room, the nurse introduces themselves, explains the procedure, and performs patient identification using two unique identifiers. Positioning is crucial: the nurse must assist the patient into an upright sitting position (high Fowler's position) or, at minimum, elevate the head of the bed to a 90-degree angle to minimize the risk of aspiration. The nurse then offers the medications one at a time if the patient has difficulty swallowing multiple pills, providing a glass of water or preferred fluid unless contraindicated. The nurse must remain with the patient at the bedside until all medication has been completely swallowed; leaving medications at the bedside for self-administration later is a dangerous practice that breaches safety protocols. If the patient is confused or attempts to hide pills in their cheek (pocketing), the nurse should gently inspect the oral cavity to ensure compliance. Finally, the nurse returns the bed to a safe, low position and ensures the call bell is within easy reach.

headings.title: Special Considerations for Vulnerable Patient Groups
headings.content: Administering oral medications to vulnerable patient groups—such as pediatric and geriatric patients—demands specialized knowledge, patience, and tailored nursing interventions. Pediatric patients often resist taking bitter or unpalatable medications and may have difficulty swallowing solid pills. Nurses can collaborate with pharmacists to obtain liquid formulations, or mix crushed, non-extended-release medications with small amounts of non-essential soft foods like applesauce or yogurt, while avoiding essential foods like milk or formula so the child does not develop an aversion to them. Precise measuring devices like oral syringes are mandatory for infants and toddlers. Conversely, geriatric patients frequently experience physiological changes such as dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), xerostomia (dry mouth), multiple chronic conditions requiring polypharmacy, and cognitive impairment. Older adults may require medications to be crushed (when safe), pills given one at a time with plenty of water, and thorough checks for drug pocketing in the buccal cavity. Additionally, age-related declines in hepatic and renal clearance mean that geriatric patients are more susceptible to drug accumulation and toxicity, requiring careful dosage adjustments and heightened vigilance by the nurse.

headings.title: Documentation and Post-Administration Monitoring
headings.content: Documentation and post-administration monitoring complete the medication administration cycle and ensure continuity of patient care. Immediately following drug administration, the nurse must accurately record the medication, dose, route, date, and exact time on the medication administration record (MAR), signing off promptly to prevent double-dosing or omissions. If a medication is refused or withheld, the nurse must document the reason (e.g., patient nausea, refusal, vomiting) in the nursing notes and report it to the prescribing clinician or charge nurse. Post-administration monitoring is equally vital; the nurse must return to evaluate the patient's therapeutic response and check for any unexpected adverse drug reactions or side effects. For instance, if an oral antihypertensive or analgesic was given, the nurse should assess the patient's blood pressure or pain score after an appropriate interval to ensure efficacy. Documenting both the administration and the patient's clinical response provides legal protection, promotes interprofessional communication, and safeguards patient safety.
